# Preface {.unnumbered} This book presents **Generative Bayesian Computation (GBC)** --- a framework for Bayesian inference, prediction, and decision-making that replaces Markov chain Monte Carlo with deep quantile neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent. The core idea is simple: if you can *simulate* from a model, you can *learn* the posterior, the predictive distribution, or the optimal decision --- all via the noise outsourcing theorem and implicit quantile networks. No likelihood evaluation, no convergence diagnostics, no chains. ## Who is this book for? {#sec-preface-audience} We wrote this book for three overlapping communities, and we have tried to make it useful to each without assuming prior knowledge from the others. **Statisticians and Bayesians** will find here a fresh computational approach to problems they already care about. If you have spent time tuning Metropolis--Hastings proposals, diagnosing $\hat{R}$ convergence statistics, or worrying about whether your variational family is flexible enough, then GBC offers an alternative that sidesteps these difficulties entirely. We develop the theory carefully, starting from the quantile function as a fundamental representation of uncertainty (@sec-quantiles), proceeding through the noise outsourcing theorem that justifies our approach (@sec-noise-outsourcing), and arriving at implicit quantile networks as the computational engine (@sec-iqn). The Bayesian inference chapter (@sec-bayesian-inference) is the pivot of the book: it shows that once you can simulate pairs $(\theta, y)$ from the joint distribution, a neural network can learn the posterior quantile function directly. You get calibrated posterior intervals for any new observation via a single forward pass. The statistics here is not an approximation --- the noise outsourcing theorem guarantees that the quantile function representation is exact. **Machine learning researchers**, particularly those working in distributional reinforcement learning, generative modeling, or uncertainty quantification, will discover that their tools have deep Bayesian roots. The implicit quantile network of @dabney2018implicit, originally designed for distributional RL, turns out to be a general-purpose Bayesian engine. We trace this connection explicitly in @sec-dist-rl, showing that the same Wasserstein contraction arguments that justify quantile temporal-difference learning also justify GBC surrogates and posterior inference. If you have implemented IQN for Atari games, you already have most of the machinery needed for likelihood-free Bayesian computation. What we add is the statistical theory --- calibration guarantees, conformal wrappers, and connections to classical Bayesian decision theory --- that turns a prediction algorithm into a principled inference framework. **Applied scientists and engineers** who use computer simulators will find practical tools that scale where Gaussian processes cannot. If you run expensive simulations --- climate models, finite-element codes, epidemiological ABMs, stochastic differential equations --- and need to quantify uncertainty in the outputs, GBC surrogates (@sec-surrogates) provide a drop-in replacement for GP emulators that trains in $O(n)$ time rather than $O(n^3)$. We devote an entire chapter to jump discontinuities (@sec-jumps), which are common in engineering simulators and notoriously difficult for smooth GP kernels. The active learning chapter (@sec-active-learning) shows how to design sequential experiments that allocate simulator evaluations where they are most needed. We have tried to make every method accessible through the `gbc` Python package with minimal boilerplate, so you can move from reading to running code in minutes. ## What makes this book different {#sec-preface-different} The standard workflow for applied Bayesian statistics is: specify a prior $\pi(\theta)$, write down a likelihood $p(y \mid \theta)$, and compute the posterior $\pi(\theta \mid y)$ via Markov chain Monte Carlo [see, e.g., @gelman2013bayesian; @robert2004monte]. This is a powerful and general framework, and we have no quarrel with the Bayesian foundations. Our quarrel is with the computation. MCMC requires evaluating the likelihood at every proposed parameter value, which is impossible for simulator-based models where the likelihood is intractable. Even when the likelihood is available, MCMC chains can be slow to mix, difficult to diagnose, and expensive to run for high-dimensional posteriors. GBC replaces the entire MCMC pipeline with a single training phase: simulate $(\theta, y)$ pairs from the prior predictive distribution, train an IQN on these pairs, and obtain posterior quantiles for any new observation by forward pass. The Bayesian answers are the same --- we are computing the same posterior --- but the computation is fundamentally different. The probabilistic machine learning textbooks by Bishop and by Murphy provide comprehensive treatments of approximate inference: variational methods, expectation propagation, and normalizing flows. These are elegant algorithms, but they require specifying and differentiating through a likelihood function or a variational family. GBC is simulation-based at its core. If your generative model is a black-box simulator written in Fortran, a stochastic agent-based model, or a system of SDEs solved by Euler--Maruyama, GBC works without modification. You need only the ability to run the simulator forward --- the neural network learns the inverse map from data to parameters. Bobby Gramacy's *Surrogates* is the closest book in spirit to ours, and we have consciously followed its conversational, code-integrated style. Where *Surrogates* builds on Gaussian process emulators for deterministic and stochastic computer experiments, we build on implicit quantile networks. The two approaches share the goal of replacing expensive simulators with fast statistical approximations, but they differ in scalability and in their treatment of distributional outputs. We compare GBC surrogates to GP emulators head-to-head on several benchmark problems throughout the book, and the results consistently favor GBC when the response surface has jump discontinuities, when the input dimension exceeds about ten, or when full predictive distributions (not just means and variances) are required. ## Notation and conventions {#sec-preface-notation} We use a consistent notation throughout the book, and we collect the most important symbols here for reference. The quantile level is always denoted $\tau \in (0,1)$, and we think of $\tau$ as a draw from the standard uniform distribution. The central object of our framework is the conditional quantile function $G^*(\tau, x)$, which maps a quantile level $\tau$ and a covariate (or conditioning variable) $x$ to the $\tau$th quantile of the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X = x$. When $x$ is a dataset $y$ and the response is a parameter $\theta$, the same object becomes the posterior quantile function $G^*(\tau, y)$ --- the $\tau$th quantile of $\pi(\theta \mid y)$. The loss function that drives all of our learning is the pinball loss, also called the check loss or the asymmetric absolute loss. For a single observation $y$ and a quantile estimate $\hat{q}$, the pinball loss at level $\tau$ is $\rho_\tau(y - \hat{q}) = (y - \hat{q})(\tau - \mathbf{1}(y - \hat{q} < 0))$. This loss penalizes overestimates and underestimates asymmetrically: when $\tau = 0.9$, underprediction is penalized nine times as heavily as overprediction. Minimizing the expected pinball loss over all $\tau \in (0,1)$ simultaneously is equivalent to learning the entire conditional distribution, a fact we prove in @sec-quantiles and exploit in every subsequent chapter. On the Bayesian side, we write $\pi(\theta)$ for the prior density on the parameter $\theta$ and $\pi(\theta \mid y)$ for the posterior density given observed data $y$. The likelihood is $p(y \mid \theta)$, and the prior predictive (marginal likelihood) is $m(y) = \int p(y \mid \theta) \pi(\theta) \, d\theta$. We emphasize that GBC never evaluates the likelihood directly --- we only require the ability to *sample* $y \sim p(\cdot \mid \theta)$ for any given $\theta$. Throughout the book, neural network parameters are denoted $\phi$ (to distinguish them from model parameters $\theta$), and we write $G_\phi(\tau, x)$ for the IQN's learned approximation to the true quantile function $G^*(\tau, x)$. ## How to read this book {#sec-preface-reading} The book has three parts, and we have designed them so that readers with different goals can chart their own path through the material. Part I (Chapters 1--5) builds the foundations that everything else rests on. We begin with a motivational overview of the GBC philosophy (@sec-introduction) and introduce the datasets that serve as running examples throughout the book (@sec-datasets). We then develop the mathematical theory: quantile functions and the pinball loss (@sec-quantiles), the noise outsourcing theorem that guarantees the existence of a quantile representation for any conditional distribution (@sec-noise-outsourcing), and implicit quantile networks that learn this representation from data (@sec-iqn). These five chapters should be read in order, as each builds directly on the previous one. Part II (Chapters 6--9) connects distributional reinforcement learning to surrogate modeling. We begin with the RL origins of IQN (@sec-dist-rl), which provides both historical context and theoretical depth. The surrogates chapter (@sec-surrogates) shows how IQN replaces Gaussian processes for computer experiments. The boundary augmentation chapter (@sec-jumps) tackles jump discontinuities that defeat smooth emulators. The active learning chapter (@sec-active-learning) develops sequential experimental design strategies. After reading @sec-dist-rl, the remaining chapters of Part II can be read in any order. Part III (Chapters 10--14) develops inference and applications. The Bayesian inference chapter (@sec-bayesian-inference) is the pivot of the entire book, showing how to perform posterior computation without MCMC. This leads naturally to generative prediction (@sec-prediction) and maximum expected utility (@sec-meu), which extend the framework to forecasting and decision-making. The causal inference chapter (@sec-causal) applies GBC to treatment effect estimation and requires @sec-bayesian-inference as a prerequisite. The calibration chapter (@sec-calibration) is the honest self-assessment: it examines when IQN fails and develops conformal and recalibration remedies. Applied readers who want to get to code quickly can skim the proofs in Chapters 3 and 4 on first reading and return to them as needed. ## Software {#sec-preface-software} All code uses the `gbc` Python package, built on PyTorch (). Installation: ```bash pip install git+https://github.com/VadimSokolov/gbc.git ``` ::: {#3fc45034 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import gbc print(f"GBC version: {gbc.__version__}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` GBC version: 0.1.0 ``` ::: ::: The package provides modules for implicit quantile networks (`gbc.iqn`), the pinball loss (`gbc.loss`), ensemble methods (`gbc.ensemble`), boundary augmentation (`gbc.augment`), active learning (`gbc.active_learning`), causal inference (`gbc.causal`), conformal calibration (`gbc.conformal`), and plotting utilities (`gbc.plotting`). Every code block in this book imports from `gbc` and can be reproduced by installing the package and running the `.qmd` source files with Quarto. ## Acknowledgments {#sec-preface-acknowledgments} This book grew from a series of research papers and graduate courses that we developed over several years at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and George Mason University.
